title: Tier II Capstone — Full Integration

pts: Communicative competence (Unit 27) reframed the goal beyond grammar; the task cycle (Unit 28) gave it a teachable structure.
Extensive input at scale (Units 31–32) and authentic materials (Unit 41) grounded the tier in real, high-volume language exposure.
Project-based and content-integrated work (Units 36–37, 45) scaled integration from single lessons to sustained, real-world-resembling work.

items: In groups, teachers lay out the twenty-four unit cards.
Sort them into three clusters: ‘aims and frameworks’, ‘integrated methodologies’, ‘assessment, motivation and diagnosis’.
Draw arrows showing which units depend on which.
Choose the three units that most changed your practice and explain why.
Display the maps and compare them across groups.
A teacher circle or DIET cluster meeting builds one shared map over two sessions.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Aims and frameworks: communicative competence (27), the TBLT cycle (28), fluency, accuracy and complexity (29), negotiation of meaning (30).

Integrated methodologies: extensive reading and listening (31–32), genre (33), cooperative learning (34), projects (36), CLIL (37), role-play (38), debate (39), presentations (40), authentic materials (41), blended learning (44).
Assessment, motivation and diagnosis: portfolios (42), peer assessment (43), communicative rubrics (46), the plateau (47), autonomy (48), error analysis (49).
A: Our strongest arrow runs from 28 to almost everything. The task cycle is where projects, CLIL and role-plays all live.

points.sub: A tool for every future decision
pts: Skehan's trilogy (Unit 29) isn't just one poster's content — it's a lens for evaluating every task designed from here forward.
Every task in Tier III and beyond can be asked: which of these three does it prioritise, and is that the right choice here?
This lens, more than any single technique, is Tier II's most transferable contribution.

v: Four tasks from your current scheme of work

items: Choose four tasks you will teach this month.
For each, rate its likely emphasis on fluency, accuracy and complexity from 1 to 3.
Ask: is that the right emphasis for this class at this point in the unit?
Adjust one condition to shift the emphasis where needed: planning time, repetition, time pressure, or a post-task focus.
Apply the three dials to a coursebook unit and discuss the balance with colleagues.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Three dials for a task (written for this book):

lines: Task: Retell a village festival story to a partner.
First telling, no planning: fluency 3 · accuracy 1 · complexity 1.
With ten minutes’ planning: fluency 2 · accuracy 2 · complexity 3.
Repeated with a new partner after a language focus on past tenses: fluency 3 · accuracy 3 · complexity 2.

blocks.x: The same task can serve different aims depending on its conditions. Research on planning and task repetition suggests that such changes shift the balance of learners’ attention (Skehan 1998; Ellis 2003). This is why Unit 29’s lens applies to every task in Parts III and IV.

body: Purpose: to present the fluency, accuracy and complexity lens as a reusable tool. Content: a control panel with three labelled dials, each set to a different position, and a teacher’s hand adjusting one. Style: clean, technical but friendly. Board version: three circles with arrows.

pts: Unit 46 made explicit what Tier I's assessment work implied: a course's assessment must measure what its methodology actually values.
Portfolio and collaborative assessment (Units 42–43) distributed that measurement across time and across people, not just the teacher alone.
This alignment between method and assessment is itself a principle to carry forward, not something specific to this tier alone.

v: One unit plan; its assessment tasks and rubrics

items: Write the three main learning aims of one unit.
List the main activities that teach each aim.
List the assessment tasks and rubric criteria that measure each aim.
Look for gaps: an aim that is taught but never assessed, or assessed but never taught.
Revise one assessment or one activity to close a gap.
Use peer and portfolio assessment (Units 42 and 43) to fill a gap where teacher assessment alone is not enough.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Aim: Learners can take part politely in a group discussion. Taught through: discussion tasks (Unit 39). Assessed through: a written test of vocabulary. → Gap.
Revision: A recorded group discussion scored with the four-band rubric (Unit 46), plus peer feedback on turn-taking (Unit 43).

blocks.x: Biggs and Tang (2011) call this constructive alignment. Unit 57 examines how well-aligned assessment can have positive washback on teaching.

points.h: Motivation at the Level It Actually Struggles
pts: Unit 47's intermediate plateau work matters beyond B1–B2 specifically — every level has its own version of stalled, invisible progress.
The response — visible evidence, micro-goals, reconnecting to purpose — generalises well beyond this one developmental stage.
Autonomy (Unit 48) is both a plateau-stage response and a durable, lifelong learning capacity worth building deliberately.

items: List the levels or classes you teach.
For each, describe what a plateau might look like (for example, Class 3 learners who can read words but not yet stories).
For each, choose one response from Unit 47: visible evidence, micro-goals, variety, or reconnecting to purpose.
Add one autonomy-building routine from Unit 48 suitable for that level.
Consider your own professional plateau as a teacher and apply the same responses.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Early primary: learners can decode but not yet read for pleasure. Response: picture books read aloud, and a reading chart with a sticker for each book.
Upper secondary: learners feel exam practice is repetitive. Response: a short project on a real local issue, and micro-goals for each practice paper.
Teachers: after ten years, lessons feel routine. Response: peer observation (Unit 68) and a small action research question (Unit 67).

blocks.x: Dörnyei (2001) argues that motivation must be maintained and protected throughout learning, not only generated at the start. The responses of Unit 47 generalize because the need for evidence that effort is working exists at every level.

body: Purpose: to show that plateaus occur at every stage. Content: a mountain path with flat stretches at different heights labelled primary, secondary, adult and teacher, with signposts reading ‘evidence’, ‘micro-goals’ and ‘why?’. Style: landscape, encouraging. Board version: a stepped line with labels.

items: None needed; this is a planning task.

pts: Unit 49 showed that error analysis grows richer, not simpler, as learners handle more complexity — a pattern that continues into Tier III.
Reading errors as evidence of an evolving system, not simple failure, remains a core interpretive principle from here forward.
This diagnostic stance is one of the clearest through-lines connecting Tier I's foundations to Tier II's methodology.

v: A class error map (Unit 49); the next unit plan

items: Take a recent class error map.
Identify one systematic pattern, one likely transfer pattern and one ‘stretching’ error.
Decide how each should affect the next unit: a language focus, a contrastive activity, or praise and patience.
Write the decisions into the unit plan.
Compare maps from Part I-level classes and B1–B2 classes to see how errors change in character.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: Three errors, three decisions (written for this book):

lines: Systematic: omitting articles before jobs. → Language focus on ‘a/an’ with jobs in the next task cycle.
Transfer: ‘although… but’. → A short contrastive activity using learners’ home-language equivalents.
Stretching: errors inside new relative clauses. → Praise the attempt; no correction yet; revisit next month.

blocks.x: This diagnostic stance, first met in Units 6 and 8 and developed in Unit 49, runs forward into Part III, where discourse and pragmatic errors (Units 52 and 53) require even closer reading.

body: Purpose: to show errors as evidence for decisions. Content: a teacher reading a learner’s page through a lens; three highlighted errors each connect by a line to a different planning note. Style: calm, analytical. Board version: three boxes with arrows.

pts: Tier II offered many methodologies — TBLT, CLIL, project-based learning, cooperative learning — not to be adopted wholesale, but combined by judgement.
Unit 25's particularity, practicality and possibility parameters apply exactly as much to choosing among Tier II's tools as they did to Tier I's.
This confirms the capstone's central claim: the toolkit grows, but the judgement it serves stays constant.

v: A class profile (Unit 25); descriptions of TBLT, CLIL, project-based and cooperative learning

items: Take the class profile you wrote in Unit 25, or write a new one.
Consider four Part II methodologies: TBLT (Unit 28), CLIL (Unit 37), projects (Unit 36) and cooperative learning (Unit 34).
For each, ask Kumaravadivelu’s three questions: does it suit these learners (particularity)? Can I manage it here (practicality)? Does it widen learners’ opportunities (possibility)?
Choose a combination for the next term and justify it in a paragraph.
Two teachers with contrasting classes justify different combinations for the same syllabus.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

blocks.x: One teacher’s justification (written for this book):

lines: Class 8C, 52 learners, fixed benches, mostly Telugu and Urdu speakers, strong interest in science. I will use short TBLT cycles every week, because they fit a 40-minute period. I will add one CLIL-style science theme each term, because learners are interested and it links English with their other subjects. I will use cooperative learning roles for bench groups of four, because the benches cannot move. I will postpone a full project until the second term, when routines are secure.

blocks.x: Prabhu (1990) argued that there is no best method and that the teacher’s own sense of plausibility matters most. Part II has given that sense more to work with.

body: Part II’s methodologies overlap more than their names suggest. A CLIL lesson often uses a task cycle, a project usually requires cooperative learning, and a debate is a kind of task. Ellis (2003) notes that tasks can be embedded in many different syllabus types, which is one reason the task cycle sits at the centre of Part II.

points.h: The Series at Its Halfway Point
pts: Tier I built the individual teacher's classroom foundations; Tier II built genuine, methodologically grounded skill integration.
Together, these fifty posters cover what most working language teachers need for confident, effective daily practice.
Tier III and IV, from here, turn toward more specialised, advanced and research-level territory.

points.h: From Tier II to Tier III
pts: Tier III goes deeper into discourse and pragmatics, genre-based writing, learner autonomy at an advanced level, full CLIL methodology, and testing and washback in depth.
These are specialisations that build directly on Tier II's foundations, not replacements for them.
The same principle holds as it did crossing from Tier I to Tier II: nothing here is discarded, only built upon.

dek: Unit 50 of 100: the series reaches its halfway point. This capstone draws all of Tier II together and opens the door into Tier III's advanced pedagogy.

aims.x: This unit closes Part II and marks the halfway point of the book. Part I built the single lesson, the unit and the course. Part II asked how the skills, tasks, materials and assessment of a course can be integrated into a coherent whole. This capstone draws those threads together, tests them against the principled eclecticism of Unit 25, and looks ahead to Part III, Advanced Pedagogy (Units 51–75).
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: summarize the main ideas of Part II and explain how they connect;
use the fluency, accuracy and complexity lens to evaluate any task;
check that a course’s assessment measures what its methodology values;
apply plateau-stage motivational responses and autonomy-building at any level;
read learner errors as evidence of an evolving system in planning decisions;
choose among Part II methodologies using particularity, practicality and possibility;
review your own practice against the first fifty units and set development priorities;
identify which Part III units build most directly on your priorities.

why: Why this matters. Tier I built the single lesson and unit; Tier II built genuine integration of skills, tasks, and assessment. Tier III now asks what expert-level practice adds on top.

background.x: Part II began from a simple observation: in real life, people rarely use one skill at a time. The model of communicative competence first proposed by Michael Canale and Merrill Swain (1980) gave the part its aim: learners need grammatical, sociolinguistic, discourse and strategic competence, not grammar alone (Unit 27). The task-based cycle, developed in different forms by N. S. Prabhu in Bangalore, by Jane Willis and by Rod Ellis (Ellis 2003), gave that aim a teachable shape (Unit 28). Peter Skehan’s (1998) distinction between fluency, accuracy and complexity provided a lens for deciding what any task is for (Unit 29).

Around these ideas Part II built a larger structure. Extensive reading and listening (Units 31 and 32) put volume of input at the centre of the programme, following the principles set out by Day and Bamford (1998). Genre awareness, cooperative learning, projects, content-based teaching, role-play, debate and presentations (Units 33–40) widened the repertoire of integrated work. Authentic materials, portfolios, peer assessment and blended learning (Units 41–44) connected the classroom with the world and with learners’ own judgement. Units 46–49 then asked whether assessment, motivation, autonomy and error analysis were keeping pace.

A principle known in curriculum design as constructive alignment (Biggs and Tang 2011) sums up much of Part II: intended outcomes, teaching activities and assessment should point in the same direction. The same principle runs through Indian policy. NEP 2020 calls for experiential, competency-based learning and formative assessment, and NCF 2023 asks for integrated, multilingual classrooms in which home languages support learning (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020; NCERT 2023). Kumaravadivelu’s (2006) parameters, introduced in Unit 25, remain the test for every choice. A task that works in a well-resourced Bengaluru school may need adapting for a Class 8 room of fifty-five in Raichur district. Part II has added to the toolkit; it has not replaced the judgement.

terms.def: The extent to which a learner’s language is free from errors in grammar, vocabulary and pronunciation; one of the three dimensions of performance, with complexity and fluency, that teachers balance in task design.
The range and sophistication of the language a learner uses, such as varied vocabulary and subordinate clauses; one of three dimensions of performance, with accuracy and fluency.
The principle that intended learning outcomes, teaching activities and assessment should all point in the same direction (Biggs and Tang 2011).
A written plan in which a teacher sets professional development goals for a period, with concrete actions, the support needed and dates for reviewing progress.
An approach in which a teacher treats learners’ errors and difficulties as evidence to be analysed in order to decide what to teach next.
The ability to speak or write at a natural speed with limited hesitation, focusing on meaning. It is often balanced against accuracy and complexity in planning tasks and giving feedback.

The capacity to take charge of one’s own learning, including setting goals, choosing materials and methods, and evaluating progress (Holec 1981); it is developed gradually, through guided choices, rather than simply handed over.

A stage, common at intermediate level, when learners feel they are no longer making progress despite effort; it can be addressed with new challenges, micro-goals and visible progress records (Richards 2008).
Combining techniques from different methods on the basis of a coherent rationale suited to the context, rather than mixing them at random.

Combining two or more language skills in one activity or sequence, as in real life, for example reading a notice, discussing it and writing a reply. Integration makes practice more meaningful and helps skills support each other.
